prompts.question: How do collision theory and Le Chatelier’s principle account for the colour change to pink when the solution is cooled? Refer to the energy profile diagram in your answer.
markerNotes: Use the energy profile to show that the forward reaction releases heat, so cooling favours it and the solution turns pink.
Collision theory needs both rates: cooling slows both, but the reverse rate falls more because the reverse reaction has the higher activation energy, Ea2.
commonStudentErrors: Describes Le Chatelier’s principle without linking the cooling to the exothermic direction.
Says cooling slows only the forward reaction, which ignores the reverse rate.
Reads Ea1 and Ea2 the wrong way round, so the reverse reaction is given the lower activation energy.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Shows how both Le Chatelier’s principle AND collision theory account for the colour change, with reference to the energy profile
4 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of how both collision theory AND Le Chatelier’s principle account for the colour change
3 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of how collision theory OR Le Chatelier’s principle accounts for the colour change
2 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of collision theory OR Le Chatelier’s principle
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: The energy profile diagram shows that the forward reaction is exothermic. Le Chatelier’s principle considers heat as a ‘substance’ that the system seeks to replace when lost. As this system is cooled, it responds in a way as to minimise the disturbance. Consequently, the forward reaction is favoured so the solution turns pink. Collision theory considers the proportion of molecules above a particular activation energy. Decreasing the temperature slows the rates of both forward and reverse reactions, due to a drop in the average kinetic energy of all particles. However, the rate of the reverse reaction decreases more than the forward reaction. This is due to a greater proportion of particles falling below the relatively higher activation energy of the reverse reaction, Ea2, as shown in the reaction profile. Since the forward reaction is faster, [CoCl₄²⁻] will decrease, and [Co(H₂O)₆²⁺] will increase, and the colour changes to pink.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by using Le Chatelier’s principle and collision theory together, with the energy profile showing the exothermic forward reaction and the larger Ea2 for the reverse reaction.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cooling removes heat from the system, so the equilibrium shifts in the direction that produces heat to replace it. The forward reaction is exothermic, so it releases heat, and the equilibrium moves forward. This forms more Co(H₂O)₆²⁺, which is pink, and the solution turns pink. The new equilibrium contains more of the pink complex and less of the blue CoCl₄²⁻ ion. The reverse reaction is endothermic, so it is disfavoured when the solution is cooled.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row with a sound Le Chatelier’s principle explanation, “The forward reaction is exothermic”, but there is no collision theory and no reference to the energy profile. Adding collision theory would lift it to the 4-mark row, and referring to the activation energies on the energy profile would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cooling the solution makes it turn pink, which shows the equilibrium has moved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by stating the observation and that the equilibrium moved. It gives no explanation, so naming the principle and the direction of the shift would lift it to the 2-mark row.

[ICE table: R row N₂H₅⁺(aq) 0.20, H₂O(l) –, H₃O⁺(aq) 0, N₂H₄(aq) 0; C row −x, –, +x, +x; E row (0.20 − x), –, x, x]
Ka = Kw / Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ = 5.88 × 10⁻⁹
Assume equilibrium concentration of N₂H₅⁺ = 0.20 mol L⁻¹ (ie, x is very small)
Ka = [H₃O⁺][N₂H₄] / [N₂H₅⁺] = 5.88 × 10⁻⁹
x² / 0.20 = 5.88 × 10⁻⁹
x = √(5.88 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.20)
x = 3.43 × 10⁻⁵ = [H₃O⁺]
pH = −log₁₀(3.43 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.46

• Infrared (IR) (Ignore any absorptions due to C—C or C—H)
• Carbon-13 NMR
• Proton NMR
• Mass spectroscopy
markerNotes: Answer each technique in turn and tie every predicted feature to a specific group or carbon, since the question asks for the link to structure.
Each ¹H signal needs its chemical shift, splitting pattern and integration, and the splitting follows the n + 1 rule from the neighbouring protons.
commonStudentErrors: Predicts the number of ¹H signals without the splitting patterns or integration.
Gives the carboxylic acid O–H as a sharp peak in the infrared spectrum, when it is broad and strong.
Predicts two ¹³C signals by treating the CH₂ and CH₃ carbons as one environment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Predicts the expected spectroscopic observations of ALL four techniques showing an extensive understanding of the relationship between molecular features and spectroscopic outcomes for these techniques
6 marks: Predicts the expected spectroscopic observations of ALL four techniques showing a thorough understanding of the relationship between molecular features and spectroscopic outcomes for these techniques
4-5 marks: Predicts the expected spectroscopic outcomes of most techniques showing a sound understanding of the relationship between molecular features and spectroscopic outcomes for these techniques
2-3 marks: Relates the expected spectroscopic outcomes of some techniques showing a basic understanding of the relationship between molecular features and spectroscopic outcomes for these techniques

sampleAnswers.answer: The infrared spectrum will show a strong, broad absorption from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ caused by the O–H of the carboxylic acid group, and a strong, sharp absorption near 1700 to 1720 cm⁻¹ from the C=O bond. The ¹³C NMR spectrum will show three signals, one for each carbon environment: the CH₃ carbon at about 5 to 40 ppm, the CH₂ carbon at about 20 to 50 ppm, and the carboxyl carbon, C=O, at about 160 to 185 ppm. The ¹H NMR spectrum will show three signals. The CH₃ protons appear at 0.7 to 2.1 ppm as a triplet with an integration of 3, because they are next to two CH₂ protons. The CH₂ protons appear at 2.1 to 4.5 ppm as a quartet with an integration of 2, because they sit next to the CH₃ group and the C=O group. The COOH proton appears at 9.0 to 13.0 ppm as a singlet with an integration of 1, because it has no neighbouring protons. The mass spectrum will show a molecular ion at m/z 74, matching C₃H₆O₂, with fragments at m/z 45 from loss of the ethyl group to give COOH⁺ and at m/z 29 for CH₃CH₂⁺.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-mark row by predicting the expected features for all four techniques and tying each one to a structural feature of propanoic acid: the O–H and C=O groups, the three carbon environments, and the 3 : 2 : 1 proton pattern.

The ¹H NMR spectrum will show a triplet at 0.7 to 2.1 ppm for the CH₃ group, a quartet at 2.1 to 4.5 ppm for the CH₂ group and a singlet at 9.0 to 13.0 ppm for the COOH proton, with integrations of 3, 2 and 1.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4–5 row by predicting the expected outcomes of three of the four techniques, with a sound link to the functional groups and the splitting. The mass spectrum is missing; adding the molecular ion at m/z 74 would extend it to all four techniques.
